{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage=  | video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUkBx-3H-Zw “Ed Cussler, 66th AIChE Institute Award Winner, on The Future of The Lecture”]}}
'''Edward L. Cussler''' (born 1940) is an American chemical engineer and professor in the department of chemical engineering and materials science at the University of Minnesota. He is internationally known for his work in fluid mechanics, transport phenomena, and gas separations,<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|url=https://www.nae.edu/27913.aspx|title=Ed Cussler|author=<!--Not stated--> |website=www.nae.edu |publisher=National Academy of Engineering |accessdate=6 May 2018}}</ref> especially in the areas of [[Synthetic membrane|membranes]] and gas [[sorption]].  Cussler is an author of more than 250 academic papers, dozens of patents, and five books including the acclaimed text: “Diffusion” (Cambridge, 2009, 3rd Edition).<ref>{{cite book|title=Diffusion|isbn = 978-0521871211|last1 = Cussler|first1 = E. L.|date = 2009-01-15| publisher=Cambridge University Press }}</ref>  He has served as director, vice president and president of the [[American Institute of Chemical Engineers]] ([[AIChE]], 1989–1995), and he presented the AIChE Institute Lecture in 2014.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.aiche.org/community/awards/institute-lecturer-award|title=AIChE Institute Award|accessdate=2 March 2018|date=2012-03-28}}</ref>  Cussler and his wife Betsy, a former teacher at [[Edina High School]], are long-time residents of Minneapolis, Minnesota.

==Early life and education==
Cussler took a B.E. degree (with honors) at [[Yale University]] in 1961 followed by an M.S. at the [[University of Wisconsin]] in 1963.  He continued towards a PhD also at Wisconsin, 1965, with his thesis entitled, "Multicomponent Diffusion in Macromolecules," where he was a student of [[Edwin N. Lightfoot]].<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://ufdcimages.uflib.ufl.edu/AA/00/00/03/83/00151/AA00000383_00151_00158.pdf|title=Minnesota's Ed Cussler|accessdate=2 March 2018|archive-date=26 January 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170126092259/http://ufdcimages.uflib.ufl.edu/AA/00/00/03/83/00151/AA00000383_00151_00158.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>  Throughout his time in school, Ed developed a love for activity with interests in running, swimming and cycling. His hobbies include cycle touring with his wife, and he has run the [[Boston Marathon]] many times.

After his PhD, he completed postdoctoral studies at the [[University of Wisconsin]] in chemical engineering.  Subsequent post-doctoral studies were completed in physical chemistry at the [[University of Adelaide]], South Australia, and [[Yale]] University in Connecticut.  In 1967, he was hired as an assistant professor in the department of chemical engineering at [[Carnegie Mellon University]], followed by promotion to associate professor in 1970 and full professor in 1973.  During his time at Carnegie Mellon University, he completed a [[sabbatical]] year at [[Unilever]] in the [[United Kingdom]].  In 1980, Ed joined the department of chemical engineering and materials science at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.aiche.org/community/bio/edward-l-cussler|title=Edward L. Cussler|accessdate=2 March 2018|date=2012-03-20}}</ref> During his time at Minnesota, Ed has taken sabbaticals at [[MIT]] and the [[University of Cambridge]].

==Honors==
Professor Cussler has received numerous honors and awards for teaching and research.  He was elected president of the [[AIChE]] in 1994. He won the 2001 [[Warren K. Lewis]] Award for Chemical Engineering Education from the [[American Institute of Chemical Engineers]].<ref name=WKLA>[http://www.aiche.org/About/Awards/WarrenKLewisAward.aspx AIChE Warren K. Lewis Award]</ref>  He was inducted into the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 2002, "For pioneering research on membrane transport in chemical and biochemical separation, and for inspiring teaching."<ref name=AAAS/> He is a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] and has received honorary doctorates from the Universities of [[Lund University|Lund]] and [[Nancy-Université|Nancy]].

On a less serious note, he received the [[Ig Nobel Prize]] in [[Chemistry]] in 2005 for an experiment settling whether people could swim faster or slower in [[syrup]] rather than water.<ref name=Ig>[http://www.improbable.com/2013/07/18/viscosity-in-the-news-twice-pitch-and-molasses/ www.improbable.com]</ref>

==Books==
Professor Cussler has authored five books in the field of chemical engineering: 
*Cussler, E.L., '''Diffusion''', Cambridge University Press, first edition, 1984; second edition, 1997; Chinese edition, 2002; third edition, 2008.
*Cussler, E. L., and Moggridge, G., '''Chemical Product Design''', Cambridge University Press, 2001; French edition, 2002; Chinese edition, 2003.
*Belter, P., Cussler, E.L., and Hu, W-S., '''Bioseparations''', John Wiley and Sons, New York, 1988.
*Baker, R.W., Cussler, E.L., Eykamp, W., Koros, W.J., Riley, R.L., and Strathmann, H., '''Membrane Separation Systems''', Noyes Data Corp., New Jersey, 1991.
*Cussler, E.L., '''Multicomponent Diffusion''', Elsevier Publishing Company, Amsterdam, 1976.
